C2. Sealing a repair feed can precede complete filling

Consider an introduced rectangular feed throat of width2mm,length10mm and height20um, supplying an initially empty.4uL damage cavity at20kPa pressure with viscosity.5Pa.s. No downstream resistance is charged, so delivery is optimistic within this model. An introduced curing layer grows inward at.2um/s from each wall:
h(t)=h0-2*v*t;
Q(t)=w*dp*h(t)^3/(12*mu*L).
The throat closes after50s. Its total preclosure delivery is
w*dp*h0^4/(96*mu*L*v)=.0666667uL,
only one sixth of the downstream cavity. A pressure-decay or external-leak observation can therefore indicate sealing while this model still contains an unfilled defect. This is not a claim about any actual resin or all repair methods.

Keeping the same feed throat uncured and open would fill the cavity in75s at5.3333nL/s. That constructive comparison requires an actual physical separation between transport and cure, a compatible trigger or protected conduit, complete mixing, temporary containment, closure and renewed access. It cannot be supplied by an ideal switch in a simulation.

If repeated repair leaves only.1um deposit per wall per event,20events reduce flow to.512 of its original value. To retain90% of initial flow after20events without cleaning, per-wall deposit must be at most17.255nm/event in this geometry. Bulk functional-stock percentage alone does not certify access; a small strategically located deposit can dominate transport. A removable sleeve, protected conduit, re-openable port, delayed reaction or different material could change the result, but each is a real renewal operation.
